conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having diarrhea for a few days now. It started with 2 or 3 a day, but now it’s up to 5 or 6. I also feel really tired and have some crampy belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no vomiting or fever. I’ve been able to eat and drink okay, though I’m not very hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I know you have Addison’s disease. Did you try increasing your prednisone when the diarrhea started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I doubled it like I did last time, but it didn’t help much this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’re going to run some blood tests to check your electrolytes and see if your adrenal insufficiency might be flaring again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak? I was worried it might be something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Low sodium and high potassium—common in Addison’s flares—can cause fatigue and cramps. We’ll know more once we get your labs back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had this before, but never with so much diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Diarrhea isn’t typical for an adrenal flare, but it can happen. We also want to rule out other causes, like celiac disease, especially since you have a history of microscopic colitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Celiac? I’ve heard of that. Could gluten be making me sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a possibility. We’ve ordered a TTG antibody test to check for celiac. In the meantime, we’re starting you on a gluten-free diet to see if it helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I can try that. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you three times your usual prednisone dose—15 mg today—to help with the flare. You’ll stay on your regular Florinef and other medications like metoprolol and Synthroid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three times? That’s a lot. Will I be on that long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for now. The endocrine team will help us taper it down. We don’t want to stay on high doses too long.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure and thyroid are okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your vitals are stable. Blood pressure is good on metoprolol, and we’re continuing your levothyroxine as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs came back. Your sodium is low at 129, and potassium is a bit high at 5.1. That confirms we’re dealing with an adrenal insufficiency flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I’ve been so tired. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if not treated, but you’re already improving. Your diarrhea has slowed, and your electrolytes are starting to stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried it wasn’t getting better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on the right track. The endocrine team recommends we lower your prednisone to 10 mg daily before discharge and keep you on the gluten-free diet for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll stay on 10 mg instead of going back to 5 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. It’s a middle ground—higher than baseline but not as high as during the flare. You’ll follow up with endocrinology next week to decide if you can taper further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. What about the celiac test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Results aren’t back yet. But since you’re improving on the gluten-free diet, it’s worth continuing until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick with it. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also giving you a short course of heparin injections to prevent blood clots, since you’re not moving around as much in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common? I’ve never had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s standard for patients staying more than a day or two, especially with chronic conditions. It’s just a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has stopped completely, and you’re feeling stronger. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking prednisone 10 mg daily, stay on your other regular meds, and continue the gluten-free diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I start feeling bad again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have persistent diarrhea, severe belly pain, nausea, or feel very weak, come back to the ER. Also, keep your follow-up with endocrinology and your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about pain? I still have some back discomfort from my old surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re prescribing a small amount of oxycodone/acetaminophen for breakthrough pain, but only use it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful with that. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—I stay on 10 mg prednisone, no gluten, and see endocrinology next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call your doctor if you’re not feeling right. You’re being discharged in good condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
